This is one of the most famous debates in economic history—the "standard of living debate" or "pessimists vs. optimists" debate. Key points:

**Pessimist view (workers were worse off or no better off):**
- Real wages were largely stagnant from ~1750 to ~1820/1840 (the "Engels pause")
- Friedrich Engels' "The Condition of the Working Class in England" (1845) documented horrific conditions
- Working hours increased dramatically; work became more regimented
- Child labor, dangerous factories, urban squalor
- Life expectancy in industrial cities declined (Manchester, Liverpool life expectancy in the 1830s was around 25-30 years in some estimates)
- Heights of workers may have declined in some periods (anthropometric evidence)
- Destruction of traditional ways of life, cottage industries, artisan independence
- Hobsbawm and Thompson (E.P. Thompson, "The Making of the English Working Class") emphasized decline in quality of life even if material wages rose slightly
- Early pessimists: Marx, Engels, the Hammonds (J.L. and Barbara Hammond)

**Optimist view:**
- Real wages did eventually rise significantly, especially after 1820-1850
- Lindert and Williamson's work in the 1980s showed real wages roughly doubled between 1820 and 1850
- Consumer goods became cheaper and more available (cotton textiles!)
- Population grew rapidly—suggesting Malthusian pressures were easing
- By 1850-1870, gains were clear
- Clapham (J.H. Clapham) was the classic optimist responding to the Hammonds

**The timing matters a lot:**
- If "first century" means ~1760-1860, then by 1860, real wages were clearly higher, and conditions were improving
- If we focus on 1780-1840, the picture is much more mixed—stagnant wages, declining urban health
- The question is whether "better off" means material living standards (wages, consumption) or broader quality of life (autonomy, health, environment, work intensity)

**Nuanced consensus-ish view:**
- Most economic historians today would say: real wages were roughly flat or slightly rising 1780-1820, then rose notably 1820-1850. So by the end of the "first century," ordinary workers were materially better off than at the start, but the gains were slow to arrive and there were significant non-monetary costs (urban disamenities, work intensity, loss of autonomy).

- Robert Allen's work on real wages shows stagnation in England until ~1820s then growth.
- Gregory Clark has argued somewhat more optimistically about living standards.
- The anthropometric evidence (heights) showed declines in the early 19th century then recovery—the "antebellum puzzle" in the US and similar in Britain.

So the honest answer to "did the Industrial Revolution make ordinary workers better off in its first century" is genuinely contested among serious scholars. There is a reasonable case for both Yes (material standards eventually rose, and comparing endpoint to start point, wages were higher) and No (the gains were minimal for decades, and quality of life in other dimensions deteriorated; for much of the first century workers were not clearly better off).
